title: What they share
hook: Torah, Shabbat, the festivals, the people and its story

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: many streams. Modern Jews organize themselves in movements, and no single one speaks for all. Did you learn one movement's name? Before we walk through them one by one, a step back. Day one thousand two hundred twelve.

A long table on a spring night. One cousin wears a black hat. Another drove in from a congregation that uses a different prayer book. A third hasn't been inside a synagogue in years. Someone at the far end has a kippah that keeps sliding off. Then the youngest child stands up and asks the question the seder sets for the youngest: why is this night different from all other nights? And every head at that table turns toward the same answer, the same story of slaves who walked out of Egypt. The streams run in different channels. Today is about the water they carry together.
screen: `ONE TABLE, MANY COUSINS.` → `WHY IS THIS NIGHT DIFFERENT?` → `THE SAME STORY.`

segments.voice: What they share. Turn it five ways, one for each finger. First, Torah. The streams read the same five books, and they hear the same line at the heart of them: "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD." They argue about how the Torah came to be and how to live it. Tomorrow is about those arguments. But the scroll in the ark is the same scroll. Second, Shabbat. "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy." One family keeps every detail of the law. Another lights candles and turns off the phones for dinner. The day is still the seventh day, and it still begins at sundown on Friday. Third, the festivals. "These are the feasts of the LORD," Leviticus says, and it lists them: Passover, the counting to Shavuot, the new year, the Day of Atonement, Sukkot. Different prayer books, same calendar. Fourth, the people. When Ruth joins her mother-in-law, she doesn't only say your God. She says "thy people shall be my people" first. In her line, belonging to a family comes before the creed. Fifth, the story. Abraham and Sarah, the slavery, the sea, Sinai, the land, the exile, the long road home. The streams tell it in different keys, and each tells it as its own. There is a Hebrew phrase for all of this together: klal Yisrael, the whole community of Israel. Not one movement. All of them. Psalm 133 says it plainly: "Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!" Unity, there, does not mean sameness. It means sitting at one table.
screen: `TORAH: THE SAME SCROLL.` · `SHABBAT: THE SAME SEVENTH DAY.` · `THE FESTIVALS: ONE CALENDAR.` · `THE PEOPLE AND ITS STORY.` · then, large: `KLAL YISRAEL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: list five shared things. Settle, and breathe. Hold up one hand, fingers open. On the first breath, fold one finger and name Torah. Then Shabbat. Then the festivals. Then the people. Then the story. Now open your hand again and go around once more, slower, and for each finger, picture one face you know, Jewish or not, who has something to do with it. A neighbor's candles. A friend's seder. Then let the hand rest in your lap. The bell holds the time.
What they share. Torah, Shabbat, the festivals, the people and its story: five things the streams of Judaism hold, even when they hold them differently. Today's word.
Your line: more in common. Today, when you notice a difference between you and someone close, go looking for one thing you share underneath it. Day one thousand two hundred twelve.

howItsDone: Jews from different movements read the same Torah, keep the same weekly Shabbat and yearly festivals, and often speak of klal Yisrael, the whole community of Israel, across their differences.

notes: Days 1202–1211 had no script files on disk when this was written; the review follows the index line for day 1211 (many streams).
Quotations are from the KJV; JPS 1917 is close for each but the KJV wording is the one quoted.
Leviticus 23 lists Shabbat, Passover, the omer and Shavuot, the first of the seventh month, the Day of Atonement and Sukkot; the teach names the festivals without numbering them. Confirm the summary.
'The scroll in the ark is the same scroll' is offered as the shared text across movements; a Keeper may want to note differing views on authorship (taken up the next day).
The hook's seder (different dress, prayer books) is an illustrative scene, not a report.
